title: The Dividing Wall
lead: In Ephesians 2:14 Christ "broke down the middle wall, the fence" between Jew and Gentile. Readers have linked the picture to the stone barrier in the Jerusalem Temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts, to the law as a fence around Israel, or to a barrier between earth and heaven.

sections.b: Josephus describes a stone balustrade in the Jerusalem Temple, with notices at intervals in Greek and Latin that no foreigner might go beyond it (Jewish War 5.193-194; 6.124-126; Antiquities 15.417). Two of the Greek notices have been found, one in 1871 and a broken piece in 1935. They warn that a foreigner who goes past will be to blame for the death that follows. The Mishnah calls the low wall the soreg (Middot 2:3). When Jews in Jerusalem accused Paul of taking Trophimus, an Ephesian, past it, a riot followed (Acts 21:27-36).

The Letter of Aristeas (probably second century BC) says Moses surrounded Israel with "unbroken palisades and iron walls" of law so that they would not mix with other peoples (Aristeas 139-142). The Mishnah tells teachers to "make a fence around the Torah" (Avot 1:1). Many scholars hold that Ephesians 2:14-15 has both in mind: the real barrier in the Temple and the law's boundary rules as a fence. Others read it as a barrier between the world below and heaven, as Gnostic writers later did.
